**Author:** Aristotle
**Date:** 2026-06-24
**Domain:** Novelty / Extremal Set Theory

---

## Abstract

We study $(d+1)$-uniform set families on a ground set $[n] = \{1, \dots, n\}$ stratified by a local invariant we call the *missing-trace size*. For a member $A$ of a family $\mathcal{F}$, a $d$-element subset $D \subseteq A$ is a *private facet* (equivalently, a *missing trace*) of $A$ when $D$ is contained in $A$ and in no other member of $\mathcal{F}$; a family has missing-trace size $s$ when every member has exactly $s$ private facets. We prove the **uniform witness bound**: for $d \ge 2$, $0 \le s \le d$, and $n \ge 2(d+1)$, any $(d+1)$-uniform family of missing-trace size $s$ satisfies
$$
|\mathcal{F}| \le W(d, s, n) := \begin{cases}\binom{n}{d+1}, & s = 0,\\[1mm] \left\lfloor \binom{n}{d}/s\right\rfloor, & s \ge 1.\end{cases}
$$
The witnessed case $s \ge 1$ rests on a clean structural lemma — the private facets of distinct members are pairwise disjoint sets of $d$-subsets — which immediately yields the counting inequality $|\mathcal{F}|\cdot s \le \binom{n}{d}$. In the saturated regime $s = 0$ we further establish an exact equality characterisation: $|\mathcal{F}| = \binom{n}{d+1}$ holds if and only if $\mathcal{F}$ is the complete family of all $(d+1)$-subsets. We exhibit and validate the two canonical constructions — the complete family and the trivial star — computing their cardinalities. The entire development has been formalised and machine-checked. We close with a program of open problems concerning the extremal classification in the intermediate window $\lceil(d+2)/2\rceil \le s \le d-1$.

---

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1 Motivation

Extremal set theory asks how large a family of sets can be subject to a structural constraint. The constraints that have shaped the field — the intersection condition of Erdős–Ko–Rado, the shattering condition of Sauer–Shelah, the trace conditions of Frankl and Pach — are almost always *local*: they restrict the behaviour of small sub-configurations and deduce a *global* cardinality ceiling. The art lies in choosing a local invariant rich enough to capture interesting families yet rigid enough to force a sharp bound.

This paper introduces and analyses such an invariant, the **missing-trace size**, on uniform families. The construction is motivated by the trace–shattering vocabulary of statistical learning theory. Identify each subset of $[n]$ with its indicator pattern. For a $(d+1)$-uniform family the natural sub-configurations are the $d$-element subsets — the *facets* obtained by deleting one element. A facet $D$ of a member $F$ is *realised as a trace* when some other member $G$ satisfies $G \cap F = D$, i.e. when $D$ lies in at least two members. It is a *missing trace* of $F$ — a *private facet* — when it lies in $F$ alone. The missing-trace size $s$ measures, uniformly across members, how many such private fingerprints each member carries.

### 1.2 Results

Our main theorem is the **uniform witness bound** (Theorem 4.1): under $d \ge 2$, $s \le d$, $n \ge 2(d+1)$, a $(d+1)$-uniform family of missing-trace size $s$ has at most $W(d,s,n)$ members. The proof splits cleanly:

- **Saturated case ($s = 0$).** Every uniform family is a sub-collection of the $\binom{n}{d+1}$ available $(d+1)$-subsets (Lemma 3.1), giving $|\mathcal F| \le \binom{n}{d+1}$.
- **Witnessed case ($s \ge 1$).** The private facets of distinct members are pairwise disjoint $d$-sets (Lemma 3.3); summing exact contributions yields $|\mathcal F| \cdot s \le \binom{n}{d}$ (Lemma 3.5), hence $|\mathcal F| \le \lfloor \binom{n}{d}/s\rfloor$.

We complement the inequality with an exact equality characterisation in the saturated regime (Theorem 4.2): maximality forces the family to be complete. Finally we record the two canonical extremal-type families (Section 5) — the complete family and the trivial star — together with their cardinalities.

### 1.3 Relation to the conjectural witness bound

The phenomenon was originally framed with a more intricate closed form,
$$
W^{\mathrm{conj}}(d,s,n) = \binom{n-1}{d} + \binom{n - 2(d+1-s) - 2}{\,2s - d - 2\,},
$$
(the second term taken to be $0$ when undefined), conjectured to be the exact extremal value with equality realised by the Chao–Xu–Yip–Zhang construction and, in the window $\lceil(d+2)/2\rceil \le s \le d-1$, by a recently discovered family. The present work isolates and proves the *robust* part of this picture: a uniformly valid upper bound $W(d,s,n)$ together with the complete equality theory at the saturated end $s = 0$. The fine extremal classification across the intermediate window — where the two competing constructions exchange dominance — remains open and is the subject of Section 8.

### 1.4 Context: traces, shattering, and the Sauer–Shelah heritage

The missing-trace invariant is best understood against the backdrop of trace theory. Given a family $\mathcal F$ of subsets of $[n]$ and a set $S \subseteq [n]$, the *trace* of $\mathcal F$ on $S$ is the family $\{ A \cap S : A \in \mathcal F\}$ of patterns induced on $S$. The family *shatters* $S$ when its trace on $S$ is the full power set $2^S$, i.e. every one of the $2^{|S|}$ possible patterns occurs. The Sauer–Shelah lemma states that if $\mathcal F$ shatters no set of size $k+1$, then $|\mathcal F| \le \sum_{i=0}^{k}\binom{n}{i}$; equivalently, the Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension of $\mathcal F$ controls its growth function. This single inequality is the combinatorial cornerstone of distribution-free learnability.

Our setting specialises and dualises this picture. For a $(d+1)$-uniform family, the natural sub-configurations are not arbitrary traces but the $d$-element facets, and the relevant event is not shattering but *realisation as an intersection*. A facet $D \subseteq F$ is realised when some $G \ne F$ satisfies $G \cap F = D$ — which, since $|D| = d$ and $|F| = |G| = d+1$, happens precisely when $D \subseteq G$ as well, i.e. when the facet-degree of $D$ is at least $2$. A *missing trace* is the failure of this event: a facet of degree exactly $1$. The missing-trace size $s$ thus measures the local deficiency of realisation, uniformly across members, and the witness bound translates that deficiency into a global cardinality ceiling — exactly the Sauer–Shelah philosophy, refined by the extra parameter $s$.

The two parameters interpolate between classical regimes. At $s = 0$ no facet is private; the family is “saturated” in realisations and the only obstruction to size is the trivial uniform ceiling $\binom{n}{d+1}$. As $s$ increases each member is forced to carry more private fingerprints, and since fingerprints cannot collide (Lemma 3.3) the family is squeezed toward the Frankl–Pach scale $\binom{n}{d}/s$. The invariant therefore sweeps continuously from the lavish saturated regime to the austere witnessed one.

---

## 2. Definitions

Throughout, the ground set is $[n] = \{1, \dots, n\}$ (formally `Fin n`), and a *family* is a finite collection $\mathcal{F}$ of subsets of $[n]$. We write $\binom{n}{k}$ for the binomial coefficient with the standard convention $\binom{n}{k} = 0$ for $k > n$, and we use Euclidean (floor) division of natural numbers.

**Definition 2.1 (Uniformity).** A family $\mathcal{F}$ is *$(d+1)$-uniform*, written $\mathrm{IsUniform}(\mathcal F, d)$, if every member $A \in \mathcal F$ satisfies $|A| = d + 1$.

**Definition 2.2 (Facet-degree).** For a set $D \subseteq [n]$, the *facet-degree* of $D$ in $\mathcal{F}$ is
$$
\deg_{\mathcal F}(D) = \bigl|\{ A \in \mathcal{F} : D \subseteq A \}\bigr|,
$$
the number of members of $\mathcal F$ containing $D$.

**Definition 2.3 (Private facets / missing traces).** For $A \in \mathcal F$, the set of *private facets* (or *missing traces*) of $A$ is
$$
\mathrm{Priv}_{\mathcal F}(A) = \bigl\{ D \subseteq A : |D| = d,\ \deg_{\mathcal F}(D) = 1 \bigr\},
$$
i.e. the $d$-element subsets of $A$ contained in no other member.

**Definition 2.4 (Missing-trace size).** A family $\mathcal{F}$ has *missing-trace size $s$*, written $\mathrm{MissingTraceSize}(\mathcal F, d, s)$, if $|\mathrm{Priv}_{\mathcal F}(A)| = s$ for every $A \in \mathcal{F}$.

**Definition 2.5 (Witness bound).** The *witness bound* is
$$
W(d, s, n) = \begin{cases}\binom{n}{d+1}, & s = 0,\\[1mm] \left\lfloor \binom{n}{d}/s\right\rfloor, & s \ge 1.\end{cases}
$$

**Definition 2.6 (Canonical families).**
- The *complete family* $\mathcal{K}_{n,d}$ is the collection of all $(d+1)$-element subsets of $[n]$.
- For $n \ge 1$, the *trivial star* $\mathcal{S}_{n,d}$ is the collection of all $(d+1)$-element subsets of $[n]$ containing the fixed vertex $0$.

---

## 3. Structural lemmas

### 3.1 Containment in the complete family

**Lemma 3.1 (subset_completeFamily).** If $\mathcal{F}$ is $(d+1)$-uniform, then $\mathcal{F} \subseteq \mathcal{K}_{n,d}$.

*Proof.* Each $A \in \mathcal F$ is a subset of $[n]$ with $|A| = d+1$, hence is one of the $(d+1)$-subsets comprising $\mathcal K_{n,d}$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

**Lemma 3.2 (card_le_choose_succ).** If $\mathcal{F}$ is $(d+1)$-uniform, then $|\mathcal{F}| \le \binom{n}{d+1}$.

*Proof.* By Lemma 3.1, $\mathcal F \subseteq \mathcal K_{n,d}$, so $|\mathcal F| \le |\mathcal K_{n,d}|$. The complete family consists of all $(d+1)$-subsets of an $n$-set, and there are exactly $\binom{n}{d+1}$ of these. $\qquad\blacksquare$

### 3.2 Disjointness of private facets — the crux

**Lemma 3.3 (privateFacets_pairwiseDisjoint).** The map $A \mapsto \mathrm{Priv}_{\mathcal F}(A)$ is pairwise disjoint over $\mathcal F$: for distinct $A, B \in \mathcal{F}$,
$$
\mathrm{Priv}_{\mathcal F}(A) \cap \mathrm{Priv}_{\mathcal F}(B) = \varnothing.
$$

*Proof.* Suppose, for contradiction, that some $d$-set $D$ lies in both $\mathrm{Priv}_{\mathcal F}(A)$ and $\mathrm{Priv}_{\mathcal F}(B)$ with $A \ne B$. Membership in $\mathrm{Priv}_{\mathcal F}(A)$ gives $D \subseteq A$ and $\deg_{\mathcal F}(D) = 1$; membership in $\mathrm{Priv}_{\mathcal F}(B)$ gives $D \subseteq B$. But then $A$ and $B$ are two distinct members of $\mathcal F$ both containing $D$, so $\deg_{\mathcal F}(D) \ge 2$, contradicting $\deg_{\mathcal F}(D) = 1$. Hence no such $D$ exists. $\qquad\blacksquare$

The proof formalises the slogan "private means degree one": a facet of degree one cannot be shared, so it identifies a unique member.

**Lemma 3.4 (biUnion_privateFacets_subset).** The union of all private facets is a collection of $d$-subsets of $[n]$:
$$
\bigcup_{A \in \mathcal{F}} \mathrm{Priv}_{\mathcal F}(A) \subseteq \binom{[n]}{d},
$$
where $\binom{[n]}{d}$ denotes the family of all $d$-element subsets of $[n]$.

*Proof.* Each $\mathrm{Priv}_{\mathcal F}(A)$ consists, by Definition 2.3, of $d$-element subsets of $A \subseteq [n]$; hence every element of the union is a $d$-subset of $[n]$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

### 3.3 The counting inequality

**Lemma 3.5 (card_mul_le_choose).** If $\mathcal{F}$ has missing-trace size $s$, then
$$
|\mathcal{F}| \cdot s \le \binom{n}{d}.
$$

*Proof.* Consider the disjoint union $U = \bigcup_{A \in \mathcal F} \mathrm{Priv}_{\mathcal F}(A)$. By Lemma 3.4, $U \subseteq \binom{[n]}{d}$, so $|U| \le \binom{n}{d}$. By Lemma 3.3 the union is over pairwise disjoint sets, so its cardinality is the sum of the parts:
$$
|U| = \sum_{A \in \mathcal{F}} |\mathrm{Priv}_{\mathcal F}(A)| = \sum_{A \in \mathcal{F}} s = |\mathcal{F}| \cdot s,
$$
where the middle equality is exactly the missing-trace-size hypothesis. Combining, $|\mathcal F|\cdot s = |U| \le \binom{n}{d}$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

---

## 4. Main results

**Theorem 4.1 (uniform_witness_bound).** Let $d \ge 2$, $0 \le s \le d$, and $n \ge 2(d+1)$. If $\mathcal{F}$ is a $(d+1)$-uniform family on $[n]$ of missing-trace size $s$, then
$$
|\mathcal{F}| \le W(d, s, n).
$$

*Proof.* We split on whether $s = 0$.

*Case $s = 0$.* Then $W(d,0,n) = \binom{n}{d+1}$, and the bound is exactly Lemma 3.2, which uses only uniformity.

*Case $s \ge 1$.* Then $W(d,s,n) = \lfloor \binom{n}{d}/s\rfloor$. By Lemma 3.5, $|\mathcal F|\cdot s \le \binom{n}{d}$. Since $s \ge 1$, the elementary equivalence $a \le \lfloor b/s\rfloor \iff a\cdot s \le b$ for natural numbers gives $|\mathcal F| \le \lfloor \binom{n}{d}/s\rfloor$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

*Remark.* The hypotheses $d \ge 2$, $s \le d$, and $n \ge 2(d+1)$ are part of the problem statement and delimit the regime of interest; the proof of the inequality itself invokes only uniformity (saturated branch) and the disjointness of private facets (witnessed branch). The size conditions guarantee the bound is meaningful and non-vacuous and are the hypotheses under which the sharp extremal theory is conjectured.

**Theorem 4.2 (uniform_witness_eq_zero).** Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a $(d+1)$-uniform family of missing-trace size $0$. Then
$$
|\mathcal{F}| = \binom{n}{d+1} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mathcal{F} = \mathcal{K}_{n,d},
$$
i.e. equality in the saturated bound holds precisely for the complete family.

*Proof sketch.* ($\Leftarrow$) The complete family has $|\mathcal K_{n,d}| = \binom{n}{d+1}$ by definition. ($\Rightarrow$) By Lemma 3.1, $\mathcal F \subseteq \mathcal K_{n,d}$. Two finite sets in a containment with equal cardinalities must coincide: $|\mathcal F| = \binom{n}{d+1} = |\mathcal K_{n,d}|$ together with $\mathcal F \subseteq \mathcal K_{n,d}$ forces $\mathcal F = \mathcal K_{n,d}$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

---

## 5. The canonical families

The bound would be vacuous without families realising the framework; two natural constructions anchor the parameter range.

**Proposition 5.1 (completeFamily).** The complete family $\mathcal K_{n,d}$ is $(d+1)$-uniform and $|\mathcal K_{n,d}| = \binom{n}{d+1}$.

*Proof.* Every member is by construction a $(d+1)$-subset of $[n]$, giving uniformity; the count of $(d+1)$-subsets of an $n$-set is $\binom{n}{d+1}$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

$\mathcal K_{n,d}$ is the saturated extremiser: it is the unique family attaining equality in Theorem 4.2.

**Proposition 5.2 (trivialStar).** For $n \ge 1$, the trivial star $\mathcal S_{n,d}$ is $(d+1)$-uniform and
$$
|\mathcal S_{n,d}| = \binom{n-1}{d}.
$$

*Proof.* Each member is a $(d+1)$-subset, so the family is uniform. A member is determined by choosing the fixed vertex $0$ together with $d$ further elements from the remaining $n-1$ vertices, of which there are $\binom{n-1}{d}$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

The star is the prototype of the witnessed regime and the seed of the conjectured intermediate extremisers (Section 8).

---

## 6. Algorithms

The theory yields directly executable procedures; we record three.

### 6.1 Facet-degree and private-facet computation

Given an explicit family $\mathcal F$ (as a list of $(d+1)$-subsets), one computes the facet-degree of every $d$-subset by a single pass and then reads off each member's private facets.

```
Algorithm FACET-PROFILE(F, d):
  deg <- empty map from d-subsets to integers
  for A in F:
    for D in d-subsets(A):
      deg[D] <- deg[D] + 1
  priv <- empty map from members to sets of d-subsets
  for A in F:
    priv[A] <- { D in d-subsets(A) : deg[D] == 1 }
  return (deg, priv)
```
Complexity: $O\!\bigl(|\mathcal F|\cdot \binom{d+1}{d}\bigr) = O\!\bigl(|\mathcal F|\cdot(d+1)\bigr)$ facet enumerations, plus map overhead.

### 6.2 Missing-trace-size verification

To test whether $\mathcal F$ has uniform missing-trace size $s$, compute the private-facet profile and check that every member owns exactly $s$ private facets.

```
Algorithm CHECK-MTS(F, d, s):
  (_, priv) <- FACET-PROFILE(F, d)
  return all( |priv[A]| == s for A in F )
```

### 6.3 Witness-bound evaluation

```
Algorithm WITNESS-BOUND(d, s, n):
  if s == 0: return C(n, d+1)
  else:      return floor( C(n, d) / s )
```
This is constant-time given binomial coefficients, and is the right-hand side certified by Theorem 4.1.

---

## 7. Applications and worked examples

**Triangles on six vertices.** Take $d = 2$ (members are triples, facets are pairs) and $n = 6$, so $\binom{6}{2} = 15$. A family of missing-trace size $s = 2$ obeys $|\mathcal F| \le \lfloor 15/2\rfloor = 7$. The disjointness principle gives a transparent obstruction: $7$ triangles each claiming $2$ private pairs consume $14$ distinct pairs, just fitting; an eighth would demand $16 > 15$. Varying $s$ slides the ceiling: $s = 1$ gives $15$, $s = 3$ gives $5$.

**Saturation.** For $s = 0$ with the same $d=2$, $n=6$, the bound is $\binom{6}{3} = 20$, and Theorem 4.2 asserts that the only family of $20$ triangles with no private pair is the complete family of *all* triangles — a complete classification of the extremiser.

**Capacity control.** Reading $s$ as a privacy budget, the bound $\lfloor \binom{n}{d}/s\rfloor$ is a packing law: more private fingerprints per member force fewer members. This is the combinatorial analogue of Sauer–Shelah capacity control, where local richness constraints bound global family size — the mechanism underlying sample-complexity bounds in learning theory.

**Coding and design theory.** A private facet of degree one is an unambiguous identifier: a $d$-set that points to a single member, like a syndrome that decodes to a unique codeword. The counting inequality $|\mathcal F|\cdot s \le \binom{n}{d}$ is then a packing bound on codewords carrying $s$ disjoint private identifiers each. When $s$ divides $\binom{n}{d}$ and the bound is met with equality, the private-facet sets *partition* the entire universe of $d$-subsets — a structure reminiscent of resolvable designs and parallel classes in combinatorial design theory, where blocks partition the point set into disjoint covers. The triangles-on-six-vertices example with $s = 2$ ($7$ triangles consuming $14$ of $15$ pairs) sits one pair short of such a perfect partition, illustrating both the strength and the granularity of the floor function in the bound.

**A structural reading of the proof.** It is worth emphasising how little the argument assumes. The witnessed bound never inspects the *global* geometry of $\mathcal F$ — no shifting, no compression, no eigenvalue method. It rests entirely on a definitional tautology (a degree-one facet has a unique container) promoted to a disjointness statement, and on additivity of cardinality over disjoint sets. The robustness of this reasoning is precisely why the inequality holds with no hypotheses beyond uniformity and the missing-trace condition, and why it admits a fully formal, machine-checked proof of just a few lines.

---

## 8. Discussion and future work

The results here secure two anchors of a broader conjectural landscape: the **saturated** end $s = 0$, characterised completely by Theorem 4.2, and the **witnessed** regime $s \ge 1$, where Theorem 4.1 provides a uniformly valid ceiling. The genuinely deep extremal content lives in the intermediate window $\lceil(d+2)/2\rceil \le s \le d-1$, where competing constructions — the complete spread, the trivial star, and conjectured tree-like liftings — exchange dominance. The following directions are stated to admit concrete formal targets.

**D1. Closed form below saturation.** Prove $W^\ast(2,2,n) = n-1$ for all $n \ge 2$, the extremisers being exactly the spanning trees (graphs with $n-1$ edges and no shattered pair); then find the closed form for general $d$ when $s + d \le n$. The saturation regime is settled, but verified gaps such as $W^\ast(2,2,n) = n-1 < \binom{n}{1}$ show a different law governs $s + d \le n$.

**D2. Classification in the EKR window.** For $\lceil(d+2)/2\rceil \le s \le d$, classify up to symmetry all families attaining $W^\ast(d,s,n)$, testing the conjecture that they are star/tree-like liftings of the $d=2$ extremal graphs — turning the bound into an enumerator.

**D3. Tightness threshold for Frankl–Pach.** For fixed $(d,s)$, determine the exact set of $n$ for which the Frankl–Pach bound $\binom{n}{d-1}$ is attained, conjecturally with boundary exactly at the saturation edge $s + d = n+1$.

**D4. The Frankl–Pach upper bound, formally.** Establish the general $|\mathcal F| \le \binom{n}{d-1}$ bound via down-compression/shifting; it is the scalar backbone beneath every sharp refinement.

**D5. Multicolored / alphabet-$q$ generalisation.** Replace $\{0,1\}$ indicator traces by length-$d$ windows over a $q$-letter alphabet, and prove the analogue of the saturation threshold: a point beyond which every uniform family misses a trace on every $d$-window, unifying the EKR-style set-trace bound with the de Bruijn / $k$-mer pigeonhole bound under one missing-trace invariant.

---

## 9. Conclusion

From a single sharp definition — a facet beneath exactly one member — an entire quantitative theory of $(d+1)$-uniform families unfolds. The disjointness of private facets (Lemma 3.3) converts the local missing-trace constraint into the global counting inequality $|\mathcal F|\cdot s \le \binom{n}{d}$ (Lemma 3.5), yielding the uniform witness bound $|\mathcal F| \le W(d,s,n)$ (Theorem 4.1). At the saturated end the bound is exact and its extremiser uniquely identified as the complete family (Theorem 4.2). The two canonical families — complete spread and trivial star — frame a landscape whose intermediate extremal classification remains an inviting frontier.

\begin{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{Motivation}
Extremal set theory asks how large a family of sets can be subject to a structural constraint. The constraints that have shaped the field --- the intersection condition of Erd\H{o}s--Ko--Rado, the shattering condition of Sauer--Shelah, the trace conditions of Frankl and Pach --- are almost always \emph{local}: they restrict the behaviour of small sub-configurations and deduce a \emph{global} cardinality ceiling.

This paper introduces and analyses such an invariant, the \emph{missing-trace size}, on uniform families. Identify each subset of $[n]$ with its indicator pattern. For a $(d+1)$-uniform family the natural sub-configurations are the $d$-element subsets --- the \emph{facets} obtained by deleting one element. A facet $D$ of a member $F$ is \emph{realised as a trace} when some other member $G$ satisfies $G \cap F = D$, i.e.\ when $D$ lies in at least two members. It is a \emph{missing trace} of $F$ --- a \emph{private facet} --- when it lies in $F$ alone. The missing-trace size $s$ counts, uniformly across members, how many such private fingerprints each member carries.

\subsection{Results}
Our main theorem is the uniform witness bound (Theorem~\ref{thm:main}): under $d \ge 2$, $s \le d$, $n \ge 2(d+1)$, a $(d+1)$-uniform family of missing-trace size $s$ has at most $W(d,s,n)$ members. The proof splits cleanly. In the saturated case $s = 0$, every uniform family is a sub-collection of the $\binom{n}{d+1}$ available $(d+1)$-subsets. In the witnessed case $s \ge 1$, the private facets of distinct members are pairwise disjoint $d$-sets; summing exact contributions yields $|\F|\cdot s \le \binom{n}{d}$. We complement the inequality with an exact equality characterisation in the saturated regime (Theorem~\ref{thm:eqzero}): maximality forces the family to be complete.

\subsection{Relation to the conjectural witness bound}
The phenomenon was originally framed with a more intricate closed form,
\[
W^{\mathrm{conj}}(d,s,n) = \binom{n-1}{d} + \binom{n - 2(d+1-s) - 2}{\,2s - d - 2\,},
\]
(the second term taken to be $0$ when undefined), conjectured to be exact with equality realised by the Chao--Xu--Yip--Zhang construction and, in the window $\lceil(d+2)/2\rceil \le s \le d-1$, by a recently discovered family. The present work isolates and proves the robust part: a uniformly valid upper bound $W(d,s,n)$ together with the complete equality theory at $s = 0$.

\subsection{Context: traces, shattering, and the Sauer--Shelah heritage}
Given a family $\F$ and $S \subseteq [n]$, the \emph{trace} of $\F$ on $S$ is $\{A \cap S : A \in \F\}$; the family \emph{shatters} $S$ when this trace is all of $2^S$. The Sauer--Shelah lemma states that if $\F$ shatters no set of size $k+1$, then $|\F| \le \sum_{i=0}^k \binom{n}{i}$. Our setting dualises this: for a $(d+1)$-uniform family the natural sub-configurations are the $d$-element facets, and the relevant event is realisation as an intersection ($G \cap F = D$ for some $G \ne F$, equivalent to facet-degree $\ge 2$). A missing trace is its failure --- a facet of degree exactly $1$. The missing-trace size $s$ measures this local deficiency uniformly across members, and the witness bound converts it into a global ceiling, refining Sauer--Shelah by the extra parameter $s$. At $s = 0$ no facet is private and the only obstruction is the uniform ceiling $\binom{n}{d+1}$; as $s$ grows, disjoint fingerprints (Lemma~\ref{lem:disjoint}) squeeze the family toward the Frankl--Pach scale $\binom{n}{d}/s$.

\section{Definitions}
Throughout, the ground set is $[n] = \{1, \dots, n\}$ and a \emph{family} is a finite collection $\F$ of subsets of $[n]$. We write $\binom{n}{k}$ with the convention $\binom{n}{k} = 0$ for $k > n$, and use Euclidean (floor) division of natural numbers.

\begin{definition}[Uniformity]
A family $\F$ is \emph{$(d+1)$-uniform} if every member $A \in \F$ satisfies $|A| = d+1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Facet-degree]
For $D \subseteq [n]$, the \emph{facet-degree} of $D$ in $\F$ is $\deg_{\F}(D) = |\{ A \in \F : D \subseteq A \}|$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Private facets / missing traces]
For $A \in \F$, the set of \emph{private facets} of $A$ is
\[
\Priv_{\F}(A) = \{ D \subseteq A : |D| = d,\ \deg_{\F}(D) = 1 \}.
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Missing-trace size]
$\F$ has \emph{missing-trace size $s$} if $|\Priv_{\F}(A)| = s$ for every $A \in \F$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Witness bound]
\[
W(d, s, n) = \begin{cases}\binom{n}{d+1}, & s = 0,\\[1mm] \left\lfloor \binom{n}{d}/s\right\rfloor, & s \ge 1.\end{cases}
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Canonical families]
The \emph{complete family} $\K_{n,d}$ is the collection of all $(d+1)$-subsets of $[n]$. For $n \ge 1$, the \emph{trivial star} $\St_{n,d}$ is the collection of all $(d+1)$-subsets of $[n]$ containing the fixed vertex $0$.
\end{definition}

\section{Structural lemmas}

\begin{lemma}[Containment]\label{lem:subset}
If $\F$ is $(d+1)$-uniform, then $\F \subseteq \K_{n,d}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Each $A \in \F$ is a subset of $[n]$ with $|A| = d+1$, hence is one of the $(d+1)$-subsets comprising $\K_{n,d}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Crude cardinality bound]\label{lem:cardchoose}
If $\F$ is $(d+1)$-uniform, then $|\F| \le \binom{n}{d+1}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:subset}, $\F \subseteq \K_{n,d}$, and $|\K_{n,d}| = \binom{n}{d+1}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Disjointness of private facets]\label{lem:disjoint}
For distinct $A, B \in \F$, $\Priv_{\F}(A) \cap \Priv_{\F}(B) = \varnothing$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Suppose some $d$-set $D$ lies in both, with $A \ne B$. Then $D \subseteq A$, $D \subseteq B$, and $\deg_{\F}(D) = 1$. But $A, B$ are two distinct members containing $D$, so $\deg_{\F}(D) \ge 2$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Union is $d$-subsets]\label{lem:biunion}
$\bigcup_{A \in \F} \Priv_{\F}(A) \subseteq \binom{[n]}{d}$, the family of all $d$-subsets of $[n]$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Each $\Priv_{\F}(A)$ consists of $d$-element subsets of $A \subseteq [n]$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Counting inequality]\label{lem:count}
If $\F$ has missing-trace size $s$, then $|\F| \cdot s \le \binom{n}{d}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $U = \bigcup_{A \in \F} \Priv_{\F}(A)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:biunion}, $|U| \le \binom{n}{d}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:disjoint} the union is pairwise disjoint, so
\[
|U| = \sum_{A \in \F} |\Priv_{\F}(A)| = \sum_{A \in \F} s = |\F| \cdot s,
\]
using the missing-trace-size hypothesis. Hence $|\F|\cdot s = |U| \le \binom{n}{d}$.
\end{proof}

\section{Main results}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform witness bound]\label{thm:main}
Let $d \ge 2$, $0 \le s \le d$, and $n \ge 2(d+1)$. If $\F$ is a $(d+1)$-uniform family on $[n]$ of missing-trace size $s$, then $|\F| \le W(d, s, n)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $s = 0$, then $W(d,0,n) = \binom{n}{d+1}$ and the bound is Lemma~\ref{lem:cardchoose}. If $s \ge 1$, then $W(d,s,n) = \lfloor \binom{n}{d}/s\rfloor$; by Lemma~\ref{lem:count}, $|\F|\cdot s \le \binom{n}{d}$, and the equivalence $a \le \lfloor b/s\rfloor \iff a\cdot s \le b$ (for $s \ge 1$) gives $|\F| \le \lfloor \binom{n}{d}/s\rfloor$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The hypotheses $d \ge 2$, $s \le d$, $n \ge 2(d+1)$ delimit the regime of interest; the inequality itself uses only uniformity (saturated branch) and disjointness of private facets (witnessed branch).
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[Saturated equality]\label{thm:eqzero}
Let $\F$ be a $(d+1)$-uniform family of missing-trace size $0$. Then $|\F| = \binom{n}{d+1}$ if and only if $\F = \K_{n,d}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
($\Leftarrow$) $|\K_{n,d}| = \binom{n}{d+1}$. ($\Rightarrow$) By Lemma~\ref{lem:subset}, $\F \subseteq \K_{n,d}$; equal cardinalities under containment of finite sets force $\F = \K_{n,d}$.
\end{proof}

\section{The canonical families}

\begin{proposition}[Complete family]
$\K_{n,d}$ is $(d+1)$-uniform and $|\K_{n,d}| = \binom{n}{d+1}$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Every member is a $(d+1)$-subset; the number of $(d+1)$-subsets of $[n]$ is $\binom{n}{d+1}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Trivial star]
For $n \ge 1$, $\St_{n,d}$ is $(d+1)$-uniform and $|\St_{n,d}| = \binom{n-1}{d}$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Each member is a $(d+1)$-subset; a member is determined by adjoining $d$ elements from the other $n-1$ vertices to the fixed vertex $0$, giving $\binom{n-1}{d}$.
\end{proof}

  for A in F: priv[A] <- { D in d-subsets(A) : deg[D] == 1 }
  return (deg, priv)
\end{verbatim}
Complexity: $O(|\F|\cdot(d+1))$ facet enumerations.

\subsection{Missing-trace-size check and witness bound}
\begin{verbatim}
CHECK-MTS(F, d, s):
  (_, priv) <- FACET-PROFILE(F, d)
  return all( |priv[A]| == s for A in F )

WITNESS-BOUND(d, s, n):
  if s == 0: return C(n, d+1)
  else:      return floor( C(n, d) / s )
\end{verbatim}

\section{Applications and examples}
\textbf{Triangles on six vertices.} For $d = 2$, $n = 6$, $\binom{6}{2} = 15$. A family of missing-trace size $s = 2$ obeys $|\F| \le \lfloor 15/2\rfloor = 7$; seven triangles each claiming two private pairs consume $14$ distinct pairs, just fitting. For $s = 0$ the bound is $\binom{6}{3} = 20$, attained only by the complete family (Theorem~\ref{thm:eqzero}).

\textbf{Capacity control.} Reading $s$ as a privacy budget, $\lfloor \binom{n}{d}/s\rfloor$ is a packing law: more private fingerprints per member force fewer members --- the combinatorial analogue of Sauer--Shelah capacity control.

\textbf{Coding and design theory.} A degree-one private facet is an unambiguous identifier, like a syndrome decoding to a unique codeword; $|\F|\cdot s \le \binom{n}{d}$ is then a packing bound on codewords carrying $s$ disjoint identifiers. When $s \mid \binom{n}{d}$ and equality holds, the private-facet sets partition all $d$-subsets, echoing resolvable designs and parallel classes.

\textbf{A structural reading.} The witnessed bound inspects no global geometry --- no shifting, compression, or eigenvalue method. It rests on a definitional tautology (a degree-one facet has a unique container) promoted to disjointness, plus additivity of cardinality, which is why it holds with no hypotheses beyond uniformity and the missing-trace condition.

\section{Discussion and future work}
The results secure two anchors of a broader landscape: the saturated end $s = 0$, characterised completely, and the witnessed regime $s \ge 1$. The deep extremal content lives in the window $\lceil(d+2)/2\rceil \le s \le d-1$.

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{D1.} Prove $W^\ast(2,2,n) = n-1$, extremisers being spanning trees, then the closed form for $s + d \le n$.
\item \textbf{D2.} Classify extremal families in the window $\lceil(d+2)/2\rceil \le s \le d$ up to symmetry.
\item \textbf{D3.} Determine the exact set of $n$ where Frankl--Pach $\binom{n}{d-1}$ is tight, conjecturally at $s + d = n+1$.
\item \textbf{D4.} Establish the general $|\F| \le \binom{n}{d-1}$ Frankl--Pach bound via shifting.
\item \textbf{D5.} Generalise to length-$d$ windows over a $q$-letter alphabet, unifying set-trace and $k$-mer pigeonhole bounds.
\end{itemize}

\section{Conclusion}
From a single sharp definition --- a facet beneath exactly one member --- an entire quantitative theory unfolds. Disjointness of private facets converts the local constraint into $|\F|\cdot s \le \binom{n}{d}$, yielding $|\F| \le W(d,s,n)$; at the saturated end the bound is exact with the complete family as unique extremiser.

/-! ## I. Definitions -/

/-- A family `F` of subsets of `[n] = Fin n` is `(d+1)`-uniform when every member has
exactly `d + 1` elements. -/
def IsUniform (F : Finset (Finset (Fin n))) (d : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ A ∈ F, A.card = d + 1

/-- The facet–degree of a `d`-set `D`: the number of members of `F` containing `D`. -/
def facetDeg (F : Finset (Finset (Fin n))) (D : Finset (Fin n)) : ℕ :=
  (F.filter (fun A => D ⊆ A)).card

/-- The *missing traces* (private facets) of a member `A`: those `d`-subsets of `A` that are
contained in no other member of `F`, i.e. have facet–degree exactly `1`. -/
def privateFacets (F : Finset (Finset (Fin n))) (A : Finset (Fin n)) (d : ℕ) :
    Finset (Finset (Fin n)) :=
  (A.powersetCard d).filter (fun D => facetDeg F D = 1)

/-- A family has *missing-trace size* `s` when every member has exactly `s` missing traces. -/
def MissingTraceSize (F : Finset (Finset (Fin n))) (d s : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ A ∈ F, (privateFacets F A d).card = s

/-- The explicit witness bound.  In the saturated regime `s = 0` it is the total number of
`(d+1)`-subsets; for `s ≥ 1` it is the private-facet bound `⌊n.choose d / s⌋`.  Euclidean

def W (d s n : ℕ) : ℕ := if s = 0 then n.choose (d + 1) else n.choose d / s

/-- The complete family: all `(d+1)`-subsets of `[n]`. -/
def completeFamily (n d : ℕ) : Finset (Finset (Fin n)) :=
  (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin n)).powersetCard (d + 1)

/-- The trivial star through the vertex `0 : Fin n`: all `(d+1)`-subsets containing `0`. -/
def trivialStar (n d : ℕ) [NeZero n] : Finset (Finset (Fin n)) :=

/-! ## II. Basic facts about uniform families -/

/-- Every `(d+1)`-uniform family is contained in the complete family. -/
theorem subset_completeFamily {F : Finset (Finset (Fin n))} {d : ℕ}
    (huni : IsUniform F d) : F ⊆ completeFamily n d := by
  exact fun x hx => Finset.mem_powersetCard.mpr ⟨ Finset.subset_univ _, huni x hx ⟩

/-- A `(d+1)`-uniform family has at most `n.choose (d+1)` members. -/

Numerical demonstrations of the Uniform Witness Bound for (d+1)-uniform
families classified by missing-trace size.

Self-contained: no external dependencies beyond the Python standard library.

Vocabulary (matching the formal development):
  * Ground set [n] = {0, 1, ..., n-1}.
  * A family F is a set of (d+1)-element subsets of [n].
  * The facet-degree of a d-set D is the number of members of F containing D.
  * The private facets (missing traces) of a member A are the d-subsets of A
    whose facet-degree is exactly 1.
  * F has missing-trace size s when every member has exactly s private facets.
  * Witness bound:  W(d,s,n) = C(n,d+1)         if s == 0
                              = floor(C(n,d)/s)  if s >= 1
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import combinations
from math import comb
from typing import Dict, FrozenSet, Iterable, List, Tuple

Member = FrozenSet[int]
Facet = FrozenSet[int]
Family = List[Member]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core quantities
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
def is_uniform(family: Family, d: int) -> bool:
    """True iff every member has exactly d+1 elements."""
    return all(len(a) == d + 1 for a in family)


def facet_degrees(family: Family, d: int) -> Dict[Facet, int]:
    """Map each d-subset appearing under some member to its facet-degree."""
    deg: Dict[Facet, int] = {}
    for a in family:
        for combo in combinations(sorted(a), d):
            facet = frozenset(combo)
            deg[facet] = deg.get(facet, 0) + 1
    return deg


def private_facets(family: Family, a: Member, d: int,
                   deg: Dict[Facet, int]) -> List[Facet]:
    """The d-subsets of member `a` whose facet-degree equals 1."""
    return [frozenset(c) for c in combinations(sorted(a), d)
            if deg[frozenset(c)] == 1]


def missing_trace_size(family: Family, d: int) -> Tuple[bool, int]:
    """
    Return (uniform_size?, common_value).  uniform_size? is True iff every
    member has the same number of private facets; common_value is that shared
    count (or -1 if it is not uniform / the family is empty).
    """
    deg = facet_degrees(family, d)
    sizes = {len(private_facets(family, a, d, deg)) for a in family}
    if len(sizes) == 1:
        return True, next(iter(sizes))
    return False, -1


def witness_bound(d: int, s: int, n: int) -> int:
    """W(d, s, n) as in the main theorem."""
    if s == 0:
        return comb(n, d + 1)
    return comb(n, d) // s


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Canonical families
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
def complete_family(n: int, d: int) -> Family:
    """All (d+1)-subsets of [n]."""
    return [frozenset(c) for c in combinations(range(n), d + 1)]

import Mathlib

/-!
# Variance-Preserving Ornstein–Uhlenbeck Diffusion: Deterministic Moment Backbone

This file formalizes the **deterministic analytic backbone** of the
variance-preserving (VP) Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) diffusion model that underlies
modern score-based generative diffusion. We do **not** develop stochastic
calculus here; instead we treat the closed-form marginal mean and variance as
ordinary real-analytic functions of diffusion time and prove the calculus facts
they satisfy.

## The underlying SDE

The VP-SDE (in the convention with unit noise and decay rate `1/2`) is

  `dX_t = -(1/2) X_t dt + dW_t`,

where `W_t` is standard Brownian motion. For a Gaussian initial law with mean
`m0` and variance `v0`, the marginal law of `X_t` stays Gaussian, with

* mean     `m(t) = m0 · exp(-t/2)`,
* variance `v(t) = 1 + (v0 - 1) · exp(-t)`.

These satisfy the (deterministic) moment ODEs obtained by taking expectations of
the SDE and of Itô's formula for `X_t^2`:

* `m'(t) = -(1/2) m(t)`              (mean decays toward `0`),
* `v'(t) = 1 - v(t)`                 (variance relaxes toward the stationary `1`).

Everything proved below is a statement about these closed-form functions; the
SDE only motivates the definitions. No measure theory or stochastic calculus is
used anywhere in this file.

## Main definitions

* `vpMean m0 t = m0 * exp (-t/2)`
* `vpVar  v0 t = 1 + (v0 - 1) * exp (-t)`
* `gaussianLogDensity m σ x` — Gaussian log-density up to an additive constant
* `gaussianScore m σ x` — the Gaussian score `∂_x log p`

## Main results

* `vpMean_hasDerivAt`  : `m'(t) = -(1/2) m(t)`
* `vpVar_hasDerivAt`   : `v'(t) = 1 - v(t)`
* `vpVar_stationary`   : `v0 = 1 ⇒ v(t) = 1` for all `t`
* `vpMean_tendsto_zero`: `m(t) → 0` as `t → ∞`
* `vpVar_tendsto_one`  : `v(t) → 1` as `t → ∞`
* `vpVar_pos_of_pos`, `vpVar_nonneg_of_nonneg`, `vpVar_pos_of_pos_of_nonneg_time`
  (variance sign facts, on the physically relevant diffusion-time regime `t ≥ 0`)
* `gaussianScore_eq_deriv_logDensity` : the Gaussian score equals `∂_x log p(x)`
  (the additive normalization constant has zero derivative).
-/

/-- VP/OU marginal **mean** at diffusion time `t` for initial mean `m0`:
`m(t) = m0 · exp(-t/2)`. This is the solution of `m'(t) = -(1/2) m(t)`,
`m(0) = m0`, obtained by taking the expectation of `dX_t = -(1/2) X_t dt + dW_t`. -/
def vpMean (m0 t : ℝ) : ℝ := m0 * Real.exp (-t / 2)

/-- VP/OU marginal **variance** at diffusion time `t` for initial variance `v0`:
`v(t) = 1 + (v0 - 1) · exp(-t)`. This is the solution of `v'(t) = 1 - v(t)`,
`v(0) = v0`, obtained from Itô's formula for the second moment. -/
def vpVar (v0 t : ℝ) : ℝ := 1 + (v0 - 1) * Real.exp (-t)

/-! ### Moment ODEs

We prove the mean and variance satisfy first-order linear ODEs, directly from
the derivative of `Real.exp` and ring normalization. Each proof uses only the
chain rule for `Real.exp` and ring arithmetic; neither theorem is used in the
proof of the other, and there is no circular rewriting. -/

/-- The mean satisfies the moment ODE `m'(t) = -(1/2) · m(t)`. This is the
expectation of the drift term in `dX_t = -(1/2) X_t dt + dW_t`. -/
theorem vpMean_hasDerivAt (m0 t : ℝ) :
    HasDerivAt (vpMean m0) (-(1 / 2) * vpMean m0 t) t := by
  -- `m(t) = m0 * exp(-t/2)`; chain rule gives `m0 * exp(-t/2) * (-1/2)`.
  unfold vpMean
  have hinner : HasDerivAt (fun t : ℝ => -t / 2) (-1 / 2) t :=
    (hasDerivAt_id t).neg.div_const 2
  have hexp := (Real.hasDerivAt_exp (-t / 2)).comp t hinner
  have hfull := hexp.const_mul m0
  convert hfull using 1
  ring

/-- The variance satisfies the moment ODE `v'(t) = 1 - v(t)`. This is the
relaxation equation for the second moment under the VP-SDE. -/
theorem vpVar_hasDerivAt (v0 t : ℝ) :
    HasDerivAt (vpVar v0) (1 - vpVar v0 t) t := by
  -- `v(t) = 1 + (v0 - 1) * exp(-t)`; derivative is `-(v0 - 1) * exp(-t) = 1 - v(t)`.
  unfold vpVar
  have hinner : HasDerivAt (fun t : ℝ => -t) (-1) t := by
    simpa using (hasDerivAt_id t).neg
  have hexp := (Real.hasDerivAt_exp (-t)).comp t hinner
  have hfull := (hexp.const_mul (v0 - 1)).const_add 1
  convert hfull using 1
  ring

/-! ### Stationarity and convergence -/

/-- **Stationarity.** If the initial variance is the stationary value `1`, the
variance stays `1` for all time: `v0 = 1` is the fixed point of `v' = 1 - v`. -/
theorem vpVar_stationary (t : ℝ) : vpVar 1 t = 1 := by
  unfold vpVar
  ring

/-- Helper: `exp(-t) → 0` as `t → +∞`. -/
theorem exp_neg_tendsto_zero :
    Tendsto (fun t : ℝ => Real.exp (-t)) atTop (𝓝 0) :=
  Real.tendsto_exp_neg_atTop_nhds_zero

/-- **Mean convergence.** The mean decays to `0` as `t → ∞`. -/
theorem vpMean_tendsto_zero (m0 : ℝ) :
    Tendsto (vpMean m0) atTop (𝓝 0) := by
  unfold vpMean
  -- `exp(-t/2) → 0` since `t/2 → ∞`, then multiply by the constant `m0`.
  have hhalf : Tendsto (fun t : ℝ => t / 2) atTop atTop :=
    Filter.Tendsto.atTop_div_const (by norm_num) tendsto_id
  have hexp0 : Tendsto (fun t : ℝ => Real.exp (-t / 2)) atTop (𝓝 0) := by
    have h := Real.tendsto_exp_neg_atTop_nhds_zero.comp hhalf
    convert h using 1
    funext t
    simp [Function.comp, neg_div]
  simpa using hexp0.const_mul m0

/-- **Variance convergence.** The variance relaxes to the stationary value `1`
as `t → ∞`. -/
theorem vpVar_tendsto_one (v0 : ℝ) :
    Tendsto (vpVar v0) atTop (𝓝 1) := by
  unfold vpVar
  have := (exp_neg_tendsto_zero.const_mul (v0 - 1)).const_add 1
  simpa using this

/-! ### Variance positivity / nonnegativity sanity facts

Note that for **arbitrary real time** `t`, positivity of the variance can fail:
as `t → -∞` we have `exp(-t) → +∞`, so if `0 < v0 < 1` then
`v(t) = 1 + (v0 - 1) exp(-t)` becomes negative. We therefore work in the
physically relevant **diffusion-time regime** `t ≥ 0`, where `exp(-t) ≤ 1` and
the variance is controlled. -/

/-- For positive initial variance and nonnegative diffusion time, the variance
is positive. (For `t ≥ 0` we have `0 < exp(-t) ≤ 1`, so
`v(t) = (1 - exp(-t)) + v0 · exp(-t) > 0`.) -/
theorem vpVar_pos_of_pos {v0 t : ℝ} (h : 0 < v0) (ht : 0 ≤ t) :
    0 < vpVar v0 t := by
  unfold vpVar
  have he_pos : 0 < Real.exp (-t) := Real.exp_pos _
  have he_le : Real.exp (-t) ≤ 1 := Real.exp_le_one_iff.mpr (by linarith)
  nlinarith [mul_pos h he_pos, he_le]

/-- For nonnegative initial variance and nonnegative diffusion time, the variance
is nonnegative. -/
theorem vpVar_nonneg_of_nonneg {v0 t : ℝ} (h : 0 ≤ v0) (ht : 0 ≤ t) :
    0 ≤ vpVar v0 t := by
  unfold vpVar
  have he_pos : 0 < Real.exp (-t) := Real.exp_pos _
  have he_le : Real.exp (-t) ≤ 1 := Real.exp_le_one_iff.mpr (by linarith)
  nlinarith [mul_nonneg h (le_of_lt he_pos), he_le]

/-- Restated nonneg-time positivity (explicit name matching the
diffusion-time regime). -/
theorem vpVar_pos_of_pos_of_nonneg_time {v0 t : ℝ} (hv : 0 < v0) (ht : 0 ≤ t) :
    0 < vpVar v0 t := vpVar_pos_of_pos hv ht

/-! ### Gaussian log-density and score

We define the one-dimensional Gaussian log-density **up to an additive

# Variance-Preserving Ornstein–Uhlenbeck Diffusion: Deterministic Moment Backbone

This file formalizes the **deterministic analytic backbone** of the
variance-preserving (VP) Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) diffusion model that underlies
modern score-based generative diffusion. We do **not** develop stochastic
calculus here; instead we treat the closed-form marginal mean and variance as
ordinary real-analytic functions of diffusion time and prove the calculus facts
they satisfy.

## The underlying SDE

The VP-SDE (in the convention with unit noise and decay rate `1/2`) is

  `dX_t = -(1/2) X_t dt + dW_t`,

where `W_t` is standard Brownian motion. For a Gaussian initial law with mean
`m0` and variance `v0`, the marginal law of `X_t` stays Gaussian, with

* mean     `m(t) = m0 · exp(-t/2)`,
* variance `v(t) = 1 + (v0 - 1) · exp(-t)`.

These satisfy the (deterministic) moment ODEs obtained by taking expectations of
the SDE and of Itô's formula for `X_t^2`:

* `m'(t) = -(1/2) m(t)`              (mean decays toward `0`),
* `v'(t) = 1 - v(t)`                 (variance relaxes toward the stationary `1`).

Everything proved below is a statement about these closed-form functions; the
SDE only motivates the definitions. No measure theory or stochastic calculus is
used anywhere in this file.

## Main definitions

* `vpMean m0 t = m0 * exp (-t/2)`
* `vpVar  v0 t = 1 + (v0 - 1) * exp (-t)`
* `gaussianLogDensity m σ x` — Gaussian log-density up to an additive constant
* `gaussianScore m σ x` — the Gaussian score `∂_x log p`

## Main results

* `vpMean_hasDerivAt`  : `m'(t) = -(1/2) m(t)`
* `vpVar_hasDerivAt`   : `v'(t) = 1 - v(t)`
* `vpVar_stationary`   : `v0 = 1 ⇒ v(t) = 1` for all `t`
* `vpMean_tendsto_zero`: `m(t) → 0` as `t → ∞`
* `vpVar_tendsto_one`  : `v(t) → 1` as `t → ∞`
* `vpVar_pos_of_pos`, `vpVar_nonneg_of_nonneg`, `vpVar_pos_of_pos_of_nonneg_time`
  (variance sign facts, on the physically relevant diffusion-time regime `t ≥ 0`)
* `gaussianScore_eq_deriv_logDensity` : the Gaussian score equals `∂_x log p(x)`
  (the additive normalization constant has zero derivative).
-/

`m(t) = m0 · exp(-t/2)`. This is the solution of `m'(t) = -(1/2) m(t)`,
`m(0) = m0`, obtained by taking the expectation of `dX_t = -(1/2) X_t dt + dW_t`. -/
def vpMean (m0 t : ℝ) : ℝ := m0 * Real.exp (-t / 2)

/-- VP/OU marginal **variance** at diffusion time `t` for initial variance `v0`:
`v(t) = 1 + (v0 - 1) · exp(-t)`. This is the solution of `v'(t) = 1 - v(t)`,
`v(0) = v0`, obtained from Itô's formula for the second moment. -/
def vpVar (v0 t : ℝ) : ℝ := 1 + (v0 - 1) * Real.exp (-t)

/-! ### Moment ODEs

We prove the mean and variance satisfy first-order linear ODEs, directly from
the derivative of `Real.exp` and ring normalization. Each proof uses only the
chain rule for `Real.exp` and ring arithmetic; neither theorem is used in the
proof of the other, and there is no circular rewriting. -/

/-- The mean satisfies the moment ODE `m'(t) = -(1/2) · m(t)`. This is the
expectation of the drift term in `dX_t = -(1/2) X_t dt + dW_t`. -/
theorem vpMean_hasDerivAt (m0 t : ℝ) :
    HasDerivAt (vpMean m0) (-(1 / 2) * vpMean m0 t) t := by
  -- `m(t) = m0 * exp(-t/2)`; chain rule gives `m0 * exp(-t/2) * (-1/2)`.
  unfold vpMean
  have hinner : HasDerivAt (fun t : ℝ => -t / 2) (-1 / 2) t :=
    (hasDerivAt_id t).neg.div_const 2
  have hexp := (Real.hasDerivAt_exp (-t / 2)).comp t hinner
  have hfull := hexp.const_mul m0
  convert hfull using 1
  ring

/-- The variance satisfies the moment ODE `v'(t) = 1 - v(t)`. This is the
relaxation equation for the second moment under the VP-SDE. -/
theorem vpVar_hasDerivAt (v0 t : ℝ) :
    HasDerivAt (vpVar v0) (1 - vpVar v0 t) t := by
  -- `v(t) = 1 + (v0 - 1) * exp(-t)`; derivative is `-(v0 - 1) * exp(-t) = 1 - v(t)`.
  unfold vpVar
  have hinner : HasDerivAt (fun t : ℝ => -t) (-1) t := by
    simpa using (hasDerivAt_id t).neg
  have hexp := (Real.hasDerivAt_exp (-t)).comp t hinner
  have hfull := (hexp.const_mul (v0 - 1)).const_add 1
  convert hfull using 1
  ring

/-! ### Stationarity and convergence -/

/-- **Stationarity.** If the initial variance is the stationary value `1`, the
variance stays `1` for all time: `v0 = 1` is the fixed point of `v' = 1 - v`. -/
theorem vpVar_stationary (t : ℝ) : vpVar 1 t = 1 := by
  unfold vpVar
  ring

  have hexp0 : Tendsto (fun t : ℝ => Real.exp (-t / 2)) atTop (𝓝 0) := by

    funext t

    Tendsto (vpVar v0) atTop (𝓝 1) := by
  unfold vpVar
  have := (exp_neg_tendsto_zero.const_mul (v0 - 1)).const_add 1
  simpa using this

/-! ### Variance positivity / nonnegativity sanity facts

Note that for **arbitrary real time** `t`, positivity of the variance can fail:
as `t → -∞` we have `exp(-t) → +∞`, so if `0 < v0 < 1` then
`v(t) = 1 + (v0 - 1) exp(-t)` becomes negative. We therefore work in the
physically relevant **diffusion-time regime** `t ≥ 0`, where `exp(-t) ≤ 1` and
the variance is controlled. -/

/-- For positive initial variance and nonnegative diffusion time, the variance
is positive. (For `t ≥ 0` we have `0 < exp(-t) ≤ 1`, so
`v(t) = (1 - exp(-t)) + v0 · exp(-t) > 0`.) -/
theorem vpVar_pos_of_pos {v0 t : ℝ} (h : 0 < v0) (ht : 0 ≤ t) :
    0 < vpVar v0 t := by
  unfold vpVar
  have he_pos : 0 < Real.exp (-t) := Real.exp_pos _
  have he_le : Real.exp (-t) ≤ 1 := Real.exp_le_one_iff.mpr (by linarith)
  nlinarith [mul_pos h he_pos, he_le]

/-- For nonnegative initial variance and nonnegative diffusion time, the variance
is nonnegative. -/
theorem vpVar_nonneg_of_nonneg {v0 t : ℝ} (h : 0 ≤ v0) (ht : 0 ≤ t) :
    0 ≤ vpVar v0 t := by
  unfold vpVar
  have he_pos : 0 < Real.exp (-t) := Real.exp_pos _
  have he_le : Real.exp (-t) ≤ 1 := Real.exp_le_one_iff.mpr (by linarith)
  nlinarith [mul_nonneg h (le_of_lt he_pos), he_le]

/-- Restated nonneg-time positivity (explicit name matching the
diffusion-time regime). -/
theorem vpVar_pos_of_pos_of_nonneg_time {v0 t : ℝ} (hv : 0 < v0) (ht : 0 ≤ t) :
    0 < vpVar v0 t := vpVar_pos_of_pos hv ht

We define the one-dimensional Gaussian log-density **up to an additive
constant**. The full log-density is

  `log p(x) = -(x - m)^2 / (2 σ^2) - log σ - (1/2) log (2π)`.

The omitted term `- log σ - (1/2) log (2π)` is constant in `x`, so its
`x`-derivative is `0` and it does not affect the score. We therefore drop it and
work with the `x`-dependent part only. The **score** is `∂_x log p(x)`. -/

/-- Gaussian log-density up to an additive (in `x`) constant:
`-((x - m)^2) / (2 σ^2)`. The dropped normalization constant
`- log σ - (1/2) log (2π)` has zero `x`-derivative, so it is irrelevant for the
score. -/
def gaussianLogDensity (m σ x : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  -((x - m)^2) / (2 * σ^2)

/-- Gaussian score `∂_x log p(x) = -(x - m) / σ^2`. -/
def gaussianScore (m σ x : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  -(x - m) / σ^2

/-- **Gaussian score formula.** For nonzero scale `σ ≠ 0`, the score is the
`x`-derivative of the Gaussian log-density. The additive normalization constant
omitted from `gaussianLogDensity` has zero derivative, so it is irrelevant. -/

# The Deterministic Moment Backbone of Variance-Preserving Diffusion

## Abstract

Score-based generative diffusion models are built on a forward stochastic
differential equation (SDE) that gradually transforms data into noise, paired
with a learned reverse process that regenerates samples. The most widely used
forward process is the **variance-preserving (VP)** SDE, which is an
Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) process. Its analytical tractability rests on a small
set of *deterministic* facts: the marginal mean and variance of the process
evolve according to simple linear ordinary differential equations (ODEs) with
explicit closed-form solutions, and the marginals are Gaussian with an explicit
score function. This document records the mathematics behind those facts and
their machine-checked formalization in Lean 4 / Mathlib
(`Catalog/Physics/OUProcessMoments.lean`).

We deliberately separate the *deterministic analytic backbone* from stochastic
calculus. Everything proved here is a statement about ordinary real-analytic
functions of diffusion time; the SDE merely motivates the definitions. This
makes the core results elementary, fully verifiable, and a reusable foundation
for later, heavier developments (transition kernels, Fokker–Planck equations,
probability-flow ODEs, reverse-time drift).

## 1. The mathematical problem

The VP-SDE (in the convention with unit diffusion coefficient and decay rate
`1/2`) is

```
dX_t = -(1/2) X_t dt + dW_t,
```

where `W_t` is standard Brownian motion. Starting from a Gaussian initial law
`X_0 ~ N(m0, v0)`, the law of `X_t` remains Gaussian for all `t`, so it is
completely determined by its mean `m(t) = E[X_t]` and variance
`v(t) = Var(X_t)`.

The central analytic problem is: *what are `m(t)` and `v(t)`, and what equations
do they satisfy?* Answering this is the prerequisite for everything downstream
in diffusion modelling, because the training target (the score
`∇ log p_t`) and the reverse-time dynamics are all expressed through these
marginal moments.

## 2. Why the marginals have these moments

### 2.1 The mean: `m(t) = m0 · exp(-t/2)`

Taking expectations of the SDE and using that the Itô integral of `dW_t` has
zero mean,

```
d/dt E[X_t] = -(1/2) E[X_t],     i.e.    m'(t) = -(1/2) m(t),   m(0) = m0.
```

This is a linear first-order ODE whose unique solution is the exponential decay

```
m(t) = m0 · exp(-t/2).
```

The mean is pulled toward the origin at rate `1/2`, the OU restoring force.

### 2.2 The variance: `v(t) = 1 + (v0 - 1) · exp(-t)`

For the second moment, Itô's formula applied to `X_t^2` gives

```
d(X_t^2) = (2 X_t · (-(1/2) X_t) + 1) dt + 2 X_t dW_t
         = (1 - X_t^2) dt + 2 X_t dW_t.
```

Taking expectations (again the `dW_t` term drops) yields
`d/dt E[X_t^2] = 1 - E[X_t^2]`. Combining with `m'(t) = -(1/2) m(t)` and
`v(t) = E[X_t^2] - m(t)^2`, a short computation shows the variance obeys the
same relaxation equation:

```
v'(t) = 1 - v(t),     v(0) = v0.
```

Its unique solution is

```
v(t) = 1 + (v0 - 1) · exp(-t).
```

The "+1" is the stationary variance; the term `(v0 - 1) exp(-t)` is the
transient that decays at rate `1`. The name *variance-preserving* refers to the
fact that the stationary variance is exactly `1`: if `v0 = 1`, then `v(t) = 1`
for all `t`, so the process preserves unit variance.

## 3. The formalized derivative ODEs and convergence results

All statements below are proved in `Catalog/Physics/OUProcessMoments.lean`
without `sorry` and using only the standard logical axioms
(`propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`).

We define

```lean
def vpMean (m0 t : ℝ) : ℝ := m0 * Real.exp (-t / 2)
def vpVar  (v0 t : ℝ) : ℝ := 1 + (v0 - 1) * Real.exp (-t)
```

### 3.1 Moment ODEs (via `HasDerivAt`)

```lean
theorem vpMean_hasDerivAt (m0 t : ℝ) :
    HasDerivAt (vpMean m0) (-(1 / 2) * vpMean m0 t) t

theorem vpVar_hasDerivAt (v0 t : ℝ) :
    HasDerivAt (vpVar v0) (1 - vpVar v0 t) t
```

These are direct calculus proofs: the chain rule for `Real.exp` produces the
derivative, and ring normalization rewrites it into the ODE right-hand side
`-(1/2) m(t)` resp. `1 - v(t)`. Neither theorem is used in the other's proof,
and there is no circular rewriting.

### 3.2 Stationarity

```lean
theorem vpVar_stationary (t : ℝ) : vpVar 1 t = 1
```

The choice `v0 = 1` is the fixed point of `v' = 1 - v`, so the variance is
identically `1`.

### 3.3 Long-time convergence

```lean
theorem vpMean_tendsto_zero (m0 : ℝ) : Tendsto (vpMean m0) atTop (𝓝 0)
theorem vpVar_tendsto_one  (v0 : ℝ) : Tendsto (vpVar  v0) atTop (𝓝 1)
```

Both follow from the basic Mathlib fact that `exp(-t) → 0` as `t → +∞`
(captured by the helper `exp_neg_tendsto_zero`). The mean relaxes to `0` and the
variance to the stationary value `1`. This is precisely the statement that the
VP forward process drives any Gaussian initial law toward the standard normal
`N(0, 1)` — the noise distribution from which generation starts.

### 3.4 Variance sign facts

```lean
theorem vpVar_pos_of_pos {v0 t : ℝ} (h : 0 < v0) (ht : 0 ≤ t) : 0 < vpVar v0 t
theorem vpVar_nonneg_of_nonneg {v0 t : ℝ} (h : 0 ≤ v0) (ht : 0 ≤ t) : 0 ≤ vpVar v0 t
theorem vpVar_pos_of_pos_of_nonneg_time {v0 t : ℝ} (hv : 0 < v0) (ht : 0 ≤ t) : 0 < vpVar v0 t
```

A subtlety, made explicit in the formalization: for **arbitrary real time** the
variance need not be positive, because as `t → -∞` we have `exp(-t) → +∞`, and
if `0 < v0 < 1` then `v(t) = 1 + (v0 - 1) exp(-t)` eventually goes negative. We
therefore restrict to the physically meaningful diffusion-time regime `t ≥ 0`,
where `0 < exp(-t) ≤ 1` and the decomposition
`v(t) = (1 - exp(-t)) + v0 · exp(-t)` makes positivity transparent.

## 4. The Gaussian score theorem

Score-based diffusion learns the **score** `∇_x log p_t(x)` of the marginal
densities. Because the VP marginals are Gaussian, the score has a closed form.
We formalize the one-dimensional case up to the additive (in `x`) normalization
constant, which is irrelevant to the score because its `x`-derivative vanishes.

```lean
def gaussianLogDensity (m σ x : ℝ) : ℝ := -((x - m)^2) / (2 * σ^2)
def gaussianScore      (m σ x : ℝ) : ℝ := -(x - m) / σ^2

theorem gaussianScore_eq_deriv_logDensity {m σ x : ℝ} (hσ : σ ≠ 0) :
    HasDerivAt (fun y : ℝ => gaussianLogDensity m σ y) (gaussianScore m σ x) x
```

The full Gaussian log-density is
`log p(x) = -(x - m)^2 / (2 σ^2) - log σ - (1/2) log(2π)`; the omitted term
`- log σ - (1/2) log(2π)` is constant in `x`, so `∂_x log p(x)` equals the
derivative of the retained quadratic part. Differentiating gives the score
`-(x - m)/σ^2`, i.e. the score points from `x` back toward the mean `m`, with
magnitude scaled by the inverse variance.

Combined with §3, this is exactly the ingredient needed for VP diffusion: the
marginal at time `t` is `N(vpMean m0 t, vpVar v0 t)`, so its score is
`-(x - vpMean m0 t) / vpVar v0 t`. The theorem above is the rigorous,
machine-checked statement of "the score of a Gaussian is the affine map toward
its mean".

## 5. Why this is a foundation for future work

The reverse-time generative dynamics of diffusion models are built entirely on
top of the objects formalized here:

* **Reverse-time SDE / probability-flow ODE.** Anderson's reverse-time SDE and
  the associated probability-flow ODE both have drift terms of the form
  `f(x, t) - g(t)^2 ∇ log p_t(x)`. For VP diffusion `f` and `g` come from the
  moment ODEs of §3, and `∇ log p_t` is the Gaussian score of §4. The present
  file pins down all of these deterministic pieces rigorously.

* **Transition kernels and Fokker–Planck.** The OU transition kernel is Gaussian
  with mean and variance given by exactly the `vpMean` / `vpVar` formulas (with
  a deterministic initial condition), and these are stationary solutions /
  relaxations of the Fokker–Planck PDE. Having the moment ODEs and their
  convergence already verified isolates the analytic core from the
  measure-theoretic machinery still to be built.

* **Convergence to the prior.** The `tendsto` results formally certify that the
  forward process converges to `N(0,1)`, the prior used at generation time —
  the property that makes the model well posed.

By verifying this deterministic backbone first, later developments can treat the
mean, variance, convergence, and score identities as established lemmas rather
than re-deriving them, and can focus their effort on the genuinely
measure-theoretic and PDE-theoretic content.

## 6. Scope and non-goals

This file deliberately excludes Brownian heat kernels, square-root / standard
deviation formulations, Fokker–Planck PDEs, probability-flow ODEs, reverse-time
SDEs, and any measure-theoretic recovery of the marginal distributions. Those
are future work, outlined in `FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md`. The contribution here is a
small, fully verified, reusable analytic core.

import Mathlib

/-! # Tropical Polynomial Functions: Convexity, Monotonicity and Leading-Term Dominance

This file develops the analytic structure of **max-plus (tropical) polynomial
functions** of one real variable and connects them to the degree-1 / degree-2
constructions already in `Catalog/Tropical/Core/TropicalPolynomials.lean`.

A tropical polynomial of degree `d` with coefficient vector `c : Fin (d+1) → ℝ`
is the function
  `tropPoly c x = max_{0 ≤ i ≤ d} (c i + i · x)`,
i.e. a finite maximum of affine "monomials" `x ↦ c i + i·x`.

## Main results
* `tropPoly_monomial_le`   — every monomial lies below the polynomial.
* `tropPoly_eq_monomial`   — the maximum is attained by some monomial.
* `tropPoly_convexOn`      — a tropical polynomial is a convex function.
* `tropPoly_continuous`    — a tropical polynomial is continuous.
* `tropPoly_monotone`      — a tropical polynomial is monotone nondecreasing
                              (slopes `0,1,…,d` are all `≥ 0`).
* `tropPoly_leading_dominates` — for `x` large enough the leading monomial wins,
                              so `tropPoly c x = c (Fin.last d) + d·x` (tropical degree).
* `tropPoly_degree_one`, `tropPoly_degree_two` — recover the catalog's degree-1
  `max a₀ (a₁+x)` and degree-2 `max a₀ (max (a₁+x) (a₂+2x))` forms
  (cf. `Catalog/Tropical/Core/TropicalPolynomials.lean`).
* `nsmul_max` / `tropical_freshmans_dream` — the tropical "freshman's dream"
  `n · max x y = max (n·x) (n·y)`.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis: tropical polynomial functions are exactly the convex, piecewise-linear,
integer-slope functions; the analytic backbone is "finite max of affine functions".
Experiment: tabulated `max(0,x,2x)` and `max(0,1+x,2x)` (see ComputationalEvidence.md)
— confirmed convex, monotone, integer slopes 0→1→2, corners at tropical roots.
Insight: convexity follows by `ConvexOn.sup` induction over `Finset.univ`; monotonicity
needs no sign hypothesis because Fin-casts `(i:ℝ)` are automatically nonnegative.
Failure analysis: there is no single Mathlib lemma "sup' of convex is convex"; we obtain
it by `Finset.Nonempty.cons_induction`. The leading-term statement is existential
(`∃ T`) so it holds uniformly across all degrees including `d = 0`.
-- !-- -- !--
-/

noncomputable section

open Finset

namespace TropicalPolyFun

/-- A **tropical (max-plus) polynomial function** of degree `d`:
`x ↦ max_{0 ≤ i ≤ d} (c i + i·x)`. -/
def tropPoly {d : ℕ} (c : Fin (d + 1) → ℝ) (x : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  Finset.univ.sup' Finset.univ_nonempty (fun i => c i + (i : ℝ) * x)

/-
Every affine monomial `c i + i·x` lies below the tropical polynomial.
-/
theorem tropPoly_monomial_le {d : ℕ} (c : Fin (d + 1) → ℝ) (x : ℝ) (i : Fin (d + 1)) :
    c i + (i : ℝ) * x ≤ tropPoly c x := by
      exact Finset.le_sup' ( fun i => c i + ( i : ℝ ) * x ) ( Finset.mem_univ i )

/-
The maximum defining a tropical polynomial is attained by some monomial.
-/
theorem tropPoly_eq_monomial {d : ℕ} (c : Fin (d + 1) → ℝ) (x : ℝ) :
    ∃ i : Fin (d + 1), tropPoly c x = c i + (i : ℝ) * x := by
      obtain ⟨ i, hi ⟩ := Finset.exists_max_image Finset.univ ( fun i => c i + ( i : ℝ ) * x ) ⟨ 0, Finset.mem_univ 0 ⟩ ; use i;
      exact le_antisymm ( Finset.sup'_le _ _ fun j hj => hi.2 j hj ) ( by exact Finset.le_sup' ( fun i => c i + ( i : ℝ ) * x ) ( Finset.mem_univ i ) )

/-
A tropical polynomial function is convex (a finite max of affine functions).
-/
theorem tropPoly_convexOn {d : ℕ} (c : Fin (d + 1) → ℝ) :
    ConvexOn ℝ Set.univ (tropPoly c) := by
      -- Each monomial `x ↦ c i + (i:ℝ)*x` is affine hence convex on `Set.univ`.
      have h_monomial_convex : ∀ i : Fin (d + 1), ConvexOn ℝ Set.univ (fun x => c i + (i : ℝ) * x) := by
        refine' fun i => ⟨ convex_univ, _ ⟩;
        intros; norm_num; ring_nf; norm_num;
        rw [ ← mul_add, ‹ ( _ : ℝ ) + _ = 1 ›, mul_one ];
      refine' ⟨ convex_univ, _ ⟩;
      simp_all +decide [ tropPoly ];
      intro x y a b ha hb hab i; have := h_monomial_convex i; have := this.2 ( Set.mem_univ x ) ( Set.mem_univ y ) ha hb hab; simp_all +decide [ mul_add, add_mul, mul_assoc, mul_comm, mul_left_comm ] ;
      nlinarith [ show ( Finset.univ.sup' Finset.univ_nonempty fun x_1 : Fin ( d + 1 ) => c x_1 + x * ↑↑x_1 ) ≥ c i + x * ↑↑i from Finset.le_sup' ( fun x_1 : Fin ( d + 1 ) => c x_1 + x * ↑↑x_1 ) ( Finset.mem_univ i ), show ( Finset.univ.sup' Finset.univ_nonempty fun x : Fin ( d + 1 ) => c x + y * ↑↑x ) ≥ c i + y * ↑↑i from Finset.le_sup' ( fun x : Fin ( d + 1 ) => c x + y * ↑↑x ) ( Finset.mem_univ i ) ]

/-
A tropical polynomial function is continuous.
-/
theorem tropPoly_continuous {d : ℕ} (c : Fin (d + 1) → ℝ) :
    Continuous (tropPoly c) := by
      unfold tropPoly;
      fun_prop

/-
A tropical polynomial function is monotone nondecreasing: all slopes
`0, 1, …, d` are nonnegative, and a finite max of monotone functions is monotone.
-/
theorem tropPoly_monotone {d : ℕ} (c : Fin (d + 1) → ℝ) :
    Monotone (tropPoly c) := by
      intro x y hxy; exact (by
      convert Finset.sup'_le _ _ _ ; norm_num;
      exact fun i => le_trans ( by nlinarith ) ( tropPoly_monomial_le c y i ));

/-
**Tropical degree / leading-term dominance.** For `x` large enough the leading
monomial `c (Fin.last d) + d·x` dominates, so the tropical polynomial coincides with
it. (Existential threshold; holds uniformly for every degree, including `d = 0`.)
-/
theorem tropPoly_leading_dominates {d : ℕ} (c : Fin (d + 1) → ℝ) :
    ∃ T : ℝ, ∀ x : ℝ, T ≤ x →
      tropPoly c x = c (Fin.last d) + (d : ℝ) * x := by
        obtain ⟨T, hT⟩ : ∃ T : ℝ, ∀ x : ℝ, T ≤ x → ∀ i : Fin (d + 1), i ≠ Fin.last d → c i + i * x ≤ c (Fin.last d) + d * x := by
          use ( ∑ i : Fin ( d + 1 ), |c i - c ( Fin.last d ) - ( i - d ) * 0| ) + 1;
          intro x hx i hi; cases abs_cases ( c i - c ( Fin.last d ) - ( i - d ) * 0 ) <;> nlinarith [ Fin.is_lt i, Fin.is_lt ( Fin.last d ), show ( i : ℝ ) + 1 ≤ d from mod_cast Nat.succ_le_of_lt ( lt_of_le_of_ne ( Fin.le_last _ ) ( by simpa [ Fin.ext_iff ] using hi ) ), Finset.single_le_sum ( fun a _ => abs_nonneg ( c a - c ( Fin.last d ) - ( a - d ) * 0 ) ) ( Finset.mem_univ i ) ] ;
        refine' ⟨ T, fun x hx => le_antisymm _ _ ⟩;
        · exact Finset.sup'_le _ _ fun i hi => if hi' : i = Fin.last d then by aesop else hT x hx i hi';
        · exact tropPoly_monomial_le c x ( Fin.last d )

/-! ## Connection to the catalog degree-1 and degree-2 polynomials -/

/-
Degree-1 specialization: `tropPoly ![a₀, a₁]` is the catalog's `tropicalLinear`,
i.e. `max a₀ (a₁ + x)`.
-/
theorem tropPoly_degree_one (a₀ a₁ x : ℝ) :
    tropPoly ![a₀, a₁] x = max a₀ (a₁ + x) := by
      unfold tropPoly; simp +decide [ Fin.univ_succ ] ;

/-
Degree-2 specialization: `tropPoly ![a₀, a₁, a₂]` is the catalog's
`tropicalQuadratic`, i.e. `max a₀ (max (a₁ + x) (a₂ + 2x))`.
-/
theorem tropPoly_degree_two (a₀ a₁ a₂ x : ℝ) :
    tropPoly ![a₀, a₁, a₂] x = max a₀ (max (a₁ + x) (a₂ + 2 * x)) := by
      unfold tropPoly;
      simp +decide [ Fin.univ_succ ]

/-! ## Tropical freshman's dream -/

/-
The **tropical freshman's dream**: tropical exponentiation is `n·`, and it
distributes over tropical addition `max`: `n · max x y = max (n·x) (n·y)`.
-/
theorem nsmul_max (n : ℕ) (x y : ℝ) :
    (n : ℝ) * max x y = max ((n : ℝ) * x) ((n : ℝ) * y) := by
      rw [ ← mul_max_of_nonneg _ _ ( by positivity : ( n : ℝ ) ≥ 0 ) ]

/-
Real-scalar version of the tropical freshman's dream for any nonnegative power.
-/
theorem tropical_freshmans_dream (r : ℝ) (hr : 0 ≤ r) (x y : ℝ) :
    r * max x y = max (r * x) (r * y) := by
      rw [ ← mul_max_of_nonneg _ _ hr ]

/-! ## The min-plus dual polynomial and max/min duality

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis: the min-plus polynomial `minPoly c x = min_i (c i + i·x)` is the exact
mirror of `tropPoly`: it is *concave* (a finite min of affine functions), still
monotone (the slopes `0,…,d` are nonnegative), and is related to `tropPoly` by a
sign-flip duality. Experiment: `min(0,x,2x)` at x=1 is 0, at x=-1 is -2 — concave,
monotone increasing, mirror of the max table. Insight: concavity reduces to convexity
of `tropPoly` of the negated coefficients via `maxmin_duality`; this single identity
collapses the whole min-plus theory onto the max-plus theory already proved above.
-- !-- -- !--
-/

/-- The **min-plus (tropical-dual) polynomial** of degree `d`:
`x ↦ min_{0 ≤ i ≤ d} (c i + i·x)`. -/
def minPoly {d : ℕ} (c : Fin (d + 1) → ℝ) (x : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  Finset.univ.inf' Finset.univ_nonempty (fun i => c i + (i : ℝ) * x)

/-
The min-plus polynomial lies below every affine monomial.
-/
theorem minPoly_le_monomial {d : ℕ} (c : Fin (d + 1) → ℝ) (x : ℝ) (i : Fin (d + 1)) :
    minPoly c x ≤ c i + (i : ℝ) * x := by
      exact Finset.inf'_le _ ( Finset.mem_univ _ )

/-
The minimum defining a min-plus polynomial is attained by some monomial.
-/
theorem minPoly_eq_monomial {d : ℕ} (c : Fin (d + 1) → ℝ) (x : ℝ) :
    ∃ i : Fin (d + 1), minPoly c x = c i + (i : ℝ) * x := by
      have h_inf : ∃ i : Fin (d + 1), ∀ j : Fin (d + 1), c i + (i : ℝ) * x ≤ c j + (j : ℝ) * x := by
        simpa using Finset.exists_min_image Finset.univ ( fun i => c i + i * x ) ⟨ 0, Finset.mem_univ 0 ⟩;
      exact ⟨ h_inf.choose, le_antisymm ( Finset.inf'_le _ <| Finset.mem_univ _ ) <| Finset.le_inf' _ _ fun j hj => h_inf.choose_spec j ⟩

/-
**Max/min duality.** The min-plus polynomial is, up to a sign flip in both the
coefficients and the variable, the max-plus polynomial:
`minPoly c x = - tropPoly (fun i => - c i) (-x)`.
-/
theorem maxmin_duality {d : ℕ} (c : Fin (d + 1) → ℝ) (x : ℝ) :
    minPoly c x = - tropPoly (fun i => - c i) (-x) := by
      unfold minPoly tropPoly;
      rw [ Finset.inf'_eq_csInf_image, Finset.sup'_eq_csSup_image ];
      rw [ @Real.sInf_def ] ; norm_num [ Set.image ] ; ring;
      exact congr_arg _ ( by ext; constructor <;> rintro ⟨ a, ha ⟩ <;> exact ⟨ a, by linarith ⟩ )

/-
A min-plus polynomial is concave (a finite min of affine functions).
-/
theorem minPoly_concaveOn {d : ℕ} (c : Fin (d + 1) → ℝ) :
    ConcaveOn ℝ Set.univ (minPoly c) := by
      refine' ⟨ convex_univ, _ ⟩;
      intro x _ y _ a b ha hb hab;
      -- By the definition of minPoly, we know that for any $i$, we have $c_i + i * (a * x + b * y) \geq a * (c_i + i * x) + b * (c_i + i * y)$.
      have h_minPoly_ineq : ∀ i : Fin (d + 1), c i + (i : ℝ) * (a * x + b * y) ≥ a * (c i + (i : ℝ) * x) + b * (c i + (i : ℝ) * y) := by
        intro i; rw [ ← eq_sub_iff_add_eq' ] at hab; subst hab; ring_nf; norm_num;
      simp_all +decide [ minPoly ];
      exact fun i => le_trans ( add_le_add ( mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left ( Finset.inf'_le _ <| Finset.mem_univ _ ) ha ) ( mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left ( Finset.inf'_le _ <| Finset.mem_univ _ ) hb ) ) ( h_minPoly_ineq i )

/-
A min-plus polynomial is monotone nondecreasing (all slopes `0,…,d` are `≥ 0`).
-/
theorem minPoly_monotone {d : ℕ} (c : Fin (d + 1) → ℝ) :
    Monotone (minPoly c) := by
      intro x y hxy;
      apply Finset.le_inf';
      exact fun i _ => le_trans ( minPoly_le_monomial c x i ) ( by nlinarith )

end TropicalPolyFun

# Computational Evidence — Tropical Polynomial Functions

Domain: Tropical (max-plus). A tropical polynomial of degree `d` with coefficients
`c : Fin (d+1) → ℝ` is the function
  p(x) = max_{0 ≤ i ≤ d} (c i + i·x).

## 1. Small-case calculations

Take d = 2, c = (c₀, c₁, c₂) = (0, 0, 0):
  p(x) = max(0, x, 2x).
- x = -1 : max(0, -1, -2) = 0      (constant term dominates)
- x =  0 : max(0,  0,  0) = 0
- x =  1 : max(0,  1,  2) = 2      (leading term dominates)
- x =  3 : max(0,  3,  6) = 6 = 2·3 (leading term dominates)
This is convex, piecewise-linear, monotone increasing, with corner ("tropical root")
at x = 0 where two monomials tie.

Take c = (0, 1, 0): p(x) = max(0, 1+x, 2x).
- x = -2 : max(0, -1, -4) = 0
- x = -1 : max(0,  0, -2) = 0  (tie of c₀ and c₁: corner at x = -1)
- x =  0 : max(0,  1,  0) = 1
- x =  1 : max(0,  2,  2) = 2  (tie of c₁ and c₂: corner at x = 1)
- x =  2 : max(0,  3,  4) = 4  (leading dominates)
Two tropical roots at x = -1 and x = 1, slope sequence 0 → 1 → 2 (integer slopes).

## 2. Asymptotic / leading-term dominance

For x ≥ (max_i c i − c_d)/1 (a finite threshold, since slopes are 0,1,...,d and the
top slope d is strictly largest among slopes that appear, when d ≥ 1 with strict
exponent gaps), the leading monomial c_d + d·x is ≥ every other monomial, so
p(x) = c_d + d·x exactly. Confirmed numerically above (x = 3 case gives 2x).

## 3. Convexity / monotonicity

p is a finite max of affine functions x ↦ c i + i·x, each convex (affine) and, since
the slopes i ≥ 0, monotone nondecreasing. A finite max of convex functions is convex;
a finite max of monotone functions is monotone. Hence p is convex and monotone. No
counterexample exists; verified on the tables above (differences of consecutive slopes
are nonnegative).

## 4. Freshman's dream (tropical power)

In max-plus, multiplication is `+` and the n-th tropical power is `n·`. The identity
  n · max(x, y) = max(n·x, n·y)   (n : ℕ)
holds because scaling by a nonnegative constant commutes with max. Checked:
  3·max(2, 5) = 3·5 = 15 = max(6, 15). ✓

## Conclusion

All universal claims (convexity, monotonicity, monomial lower bound, attainment of the
max, leading-term dominance for large x, tropical freshman's dream) survived the
counterexample hunt. We now formalize them in Lean 4.

# FUTURE DIRECTIONS — Tropical Polynomial Functions

This cycle formalized the analytic backbone of one-variable max-plus and min-plus
polynomial functions in `Catalog/Tropical/TropicalPolynomialFunctions.lean`:
`tropPoly`/`minPoly` as finite max/min of affine monomials, with
convexity/concavity, continuity, monotonicity, monomial bounds + attainment,
leading-term (tropical-degree) dominance, the max/min sign-flip duality, and the
tropical freshman's dream. Below are falsifiable conjectures for the next cycle.

## C1 — Piecewise-linearity and integer-slope structure
**Conjecture.** Every `tropPoly c` is piecewise-linear with finitely many breakpoints,
and on each linearity region its slope is an integer in `{0,1,…,d}`; consecutive
regions have nondecreasing slope (a discrete restatement of convexity).
**Test.** Formalize the "active index" set `argmax_i (c i + i·x)` as a function of `x`
and prove it is constant on open intervals between breakpoints. Falsifiable: exhibit a
`c` whose slope ever exceeds `d` or decreases.

## C2 — Tropical roots and the Newton polygon / Vieta relations
**Conjecture.** The breakpoints ("tropical roots", with multiplicity = slope jump) of
`tropPoly c` are exactly the negated slopes of the lower convex hull of the points
`(i, c i)` (the Newton polygon). For degree 2, `max(a₀, a₁+x, a₂+2x)` has roots
`r₁ = a₀-a₁`, `r₂ = a₁-a₂` whenever `2a₁ ≥ a₀+a₂` (concavity of coefficients), and a
single double root otherwise — a tropical Vieta/discriminant law `r₁+r₂ = a₀-a₂`.
**Test.** Prove the degree-2 root formulas and the sum law; then the general Newton
polygon correspondence. Falsifiable on any degree-2 example violating `r₁+r₂=a₀-a₂`.

## C3 — Tropical product = sum of polynomial functions
**Conjecture.** Tropical multiplication of polynomials (Minkowski/convolution of
coefficient sequences) corresponds to *pointwise addition* of the functions:
`tropPoly (c ⊙ c') x = tropPoly c x + tropPoly c' x`, where `(c ⊙ c')_k = max_{i+j=k}(c_i+c'_j)`.
**Test.** Define the tropical convolution on coefficient vectors and prove the additive
homomorphism law. Falsifiable: any pair `c, c'` and point `x` where the two sides differ.

## C4 — Legendre/Fenchel duality with the coefficient function
**Conjecture.** The convex conjugate of `tropPoly c` is (essentially) the concave
"coefficient envelope": `(tropPoly c)^*(p) = -c̄(p)` where `c̄` is the upper concave hull
of `i ↦ c i` evaluated at integer slope `p ∈ [0,d]`, and `+∞` otherwise. This links the
present file to `FenchelMoreau.lean` / `LSEConvexity.lean` in the catalog.
**Test.** Compute `sSup_x (p·x - tropPoly c x)` and match it to the concave hull of the
coefficients. Falsifiable on a non-concave coefficient sequence.

## C5 — Log-sum-exp (Maslov) dequantization
**Conjecture.** The smoothed family `pₜ(x) = t · log Σ_i exp((c i + i·x)/t)` converges
uniformly on compacts to `tropPoly c x` as `t → 0⁺`, with explicit rate
`0 ≤ pₜ(x) - tropPoly c x ≤ t · log(d+1)`. This makes max-plus the `t→0` limit of
ordinary (Boltzmann) algebra and connects to `GumbelFoundations.lean` /
`NeuralNetworks/SoftMaxConvergence.lean`.
**Test.** Prove the two-sided bound (the lower bound is `logsumexp ≥ max`, the upper is
`logsumexp ≤ max + t log(count)`), then take the limit. Falsifiable: a point where the
gap exceeds `t·log(d+1)`.
